summary: This note is a long encyclopedic overview of proteins as biomolecules: their functions, amino acid chain structure, history of discovery, synthesis via genes and ribosomes, levels of structure, classes, and experimental study. It covers how proteins fold into 3D shapes that determine activity, how they act as enzymes, signaling molecules, transporters and structural components, and how their evolution and purification and analysis methods work. The text is cut off mid-passage in the purification section.
one_line: Overview of proteins as amino acid polymers: their structure, biosynthesis, functions as enzymes and structural molecules, history, and study methods.
key_facts: Proteins comprise one or more long chains of amino acid residues and perform functions including catalysing metabolic reactions, DNA replication, responding to stimuli, providing structure, and transporting molecules.
A linear chain of amino acid residues is called a polypeptide; short polypeptides under about 20–30 residues are commonly called peptides.
The genetic code specifies 20 standard amino acids, though selenocysteine and, in certain archaea, pyrrolysine can also be included.
The average lifespan of a protein in mammalian cells is 1–2 days.
Proteins were named by Jöns Jacob Berzelius in 1838, derived from the Greek word proteios meaning 'primary'.
The first protein to be sequenced was insulin, by Frederick Sanger, in 1949; he won the Nobel Prize for this achievement in 1958.
The first protein structures solved by X-ray crystallography were hemoglobin by Max Perutz and myoglobin by John Kendrew, in 1958.
As of 2017, the Protein Data Bank had over 126,060 atomic-resolution structures of proteins.
James B. Sumner showed in 1926 that the enzyme urease was a protein.
In the 1950s, the Armour Hot Dog Co. purified 1 kg of pure bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A and made it freely available to scientists.
Most proteins consist of linear polymers built from up to 20 different L-α-amino acids; proline is the only one differing from the basic structure.
The rate of protein synthesis in prokaryotes can reach up to 20 amino acids per second.
The largest known proteins are the titins, with a molecular mass of almost 3,000 kDa and a length of almost 27,000 amino acids.
Chemical synthesis is inefficient for polypeptides longer than about 300 amino acids.
Orotate decarboxylase shows enzymatic rate acceleration of as much as 10-fold: 78 million years without the enzyme, 18 milliseconds with it.
Human cells contain on the order of 1 to 3 billion proteins, while the human genome encodes about 20,000 proteins of which only 6,000 are detected in lymphoblastoid cells.
